title: 10 Finance Interview Formulas
subtitle: Revenue → FCF → EV → share price - one connected chain
openingQuestion: You already have a stock's EPS and P/E. What is still missing before you can get to Enterprise Value?
openingOptions: The company's debt and its cash
Nothing - multiply EPS by P/E by the share count and that is EV
Revenue and cost of goods sold for the period
The dividend payout ratio for the last three years
explanation: EPS times P/E gives the price per share, and multiplying by the share count gives Market Cap - the part that belongs to shareholders. Enterprise Value is what it costs to buy the WHOLE business, so you add debt and subtract cash: the buyer takes on that debt, and gets to use that cash. Two companies with the same Market Cap, one carrying 10,000bn of net debt and the other holding 10,000bn of net cash, have Enterprise Values 20,000bn apart. That is why comparing two companies on P/E can give you the opposite conclusion from comparing them on EV/EBITDA.

realWorldExample.description: Revenue around 55,000bn, EBITDA around 9,000bn, net income around 6,500bn, EPS around 5,000 dong. At a market P/E of about 20x that puts the price near 100,000 dong - the same chain of formulas, run from the top line all the way down to the share price.

sections.text: Every finance interview - IB, PE, equity research, corporate finance - asks about these ten formulas. But the real question is never "what is the formula". It is "why does it matter" and "when do you use which one".

What matters more than memorising each formula is seeing how they link into one chain: from Revenue down to FCF, then from FCF up to Enterprise Value, then from EV back to the price of a single share. Someone holding ten disconnected formulas stalls on the second question; someone who sees the chain can re-derive the formula they forgot.
The chain from Revenue down to FCF

items: + D&A (added back, because it is a non-cash charge)

sections.label: Where people slip
sections.text: D&A is subtracted once at EBIT and added back once at OCF. That is not double counting: it comes out because the income statement has to recognise the wear on the asset, and it goes back in because no actual cash left the business this period.

sections.title: From the top line to the share price

variables.name: Gross Profit = Revenue − COGS
variables.description: Gross margin = GP/Revenue. A high one means real pricing power, or low production cost.

variables.name: EBITDA = Gross Profit − Operating Expenses
variables.description: A rough stand-in for cash generated by operations. Used heavily in M&A through the EV/EBITDA multiple.

variables.name: EBIT = EBITDA − D&A
variables.description: Earnings before interest and tax. Reflects operating performance, independent of capital structure.

variables.name: Net Income = (EBIT − Interest) × (1 − Tax Rate)
variables.description: The bottom line for shareholders. But be careful: it is heavily shaped by accounting choices.

variables.name: Free Cash Flow = OCF − CapEx
variables.description: The genuinely free cash. This is the basis of every DCF, and what Buffett calls "owner earnings".

variables.name: Enterprise Value = Market Cap + Total Debt − Cash
variables.description: What it really costs to buy the whole business. Comparable across companies with different capital structures.

variables.name: Equity Value = EV − Net Debt
variables.description: The shareholders' share. Divide by the share count for a theoretical price per share.

variables.name: P/E = Price per Share / EPS
variables.description: How much an investor pays for one unit of profit. A high P/E usually means high growth expectations.

variables.name: EV/EBITDA = Enterprise Value / EBITDA
variables.description: The most common multiple in M&A. Neutral to leverage and to depreciation policy.

variables.name: EPS = Net Income / Diluted Shares
variables.description: Use diluted shares, which include options and warrants - not the shares currently outstanding.

items: Market P/E of about 20x → price near 100,000 dong
EV/EBITDA around 15x, the usual range for Vietnamese technology names

quiz.question: What does a gross profit margin of 40% mean?
options: Revenue this period grew 40% against the same period last year
40 dong of profit is left of every 100 dong of revenue after all costs
40 dong is left of every 100 dong of revenue after cost of goods
Marketing spend accounted for 40% of revenue in the period
quiz.explanation: Gross Profit = Revenue − COGS, and GPM = GP/Revenue. 40% means 60% of revenue went on direct production or purchase costs. This is the GROSS margin - before selling costs, admin, interest and tax. Confusing it with the net margin is the single most common slip.

quiz.question: What is the difference between EBITDA and EBIT?
options: EBITDA adds tax back to EBIT
EBIT is for manufacturers, EBITDA is for technology
The two are the same, just named differently
EBITDA adds D&A back to EBIT
quiz.explanation: EBITDA = EBIT + D&A. D&A is a non-cash charge - the wear on assets - so adding it back gets you closer to the cash the business generates. That is why EV/EBITDA is used to compare businesses with very different levels of fixed-asset investment.

quiz.question: What does Enterprise Value equal?
options: Market Cap plus total debt minus cash
Total assets on the balance sheet
Market Cap plus total debt plus cash
Net income times the market's P/E
quiz.explanation: EV = Market Cap + Total Debt − Cash. Whoever buys the whole business takes on the debt and gets to use the cash, so debt is added and cash is subtracted. Adding cash instead of subtracting it is a common sign flip, and it inflates the EV of any cash-rich business.

quiz.question: P/E is 25x and EPS is 4,000 dong. What is the share price?
options: 6,250 dong (divided the wrong way round)
16,000 dong (= 4,000 × 4, wrong multiplier)
4,025 dong (= 4,000 + 25, added instead of multiplied)
quiz.explanation: P/E = Price / EPS, so Price = P/E × EPS = 25 × 4,000 = 100,000 dong. Remembering which way the division goes is enough to avoid inverting it: P/E says "how much you pay for one unit of profit", so it is price over profit.

quiz.question: Why do analysts use EV/EBITDA instead of P/E?
options: Because EV/EBITDA is always lower than P/E, so the multiple looks better
Because EBITDA is easier to compute than net income, so it saves time
Because it is neutral to capital structure and depreciation policy
Because P/E does not apply to Vietnamese companies
quiz.explanation: EV includes debt, so leverage does not distort the multiple, and EBITDA sits above D&A, so depreciation policy does not distort it either. Those two properties are what let you compare companies with different capital structures, or value an M&A deal where the capital structure will change after the purchase.

practicePrompt.question: Two companies both have a Market Cap of 10,000bn and EBITDA of 1,000bn. Company A carries 5,000bn of net debt; company B holds 2,000bn of net cash. On EV/EBITDA, which one is the market paying more for?
options: Company A, because A's EV is 15,000bn, a multiple of 15x
Company B, because B's EV is 12,000bn, a multiple of 12x
Neither - same Market Cap and same EBITDA means the same multiple
Company B, because more cash makes it worth more
practicePrompt.explanation: A's EV = 10,000 + 5,000 = 15,000bn, or 15x EBITDA. B's EV = 10,000 − 2,000 = 8,000bn, or 8x. Same Market Cap, same EBITDA, and the multiples are nearly double apart - which is exactly what P/E cannot see. The 12,000bn option is the sign flip: adding cash instead of subtracting it.

keyTakeaways: Revenue → Gross Profit → EBITDA → EBIT → Net Income → OCF → FCF is one connected chain, not seven separate formulas.
EV = Market Cap + Debt − Cash: debt is added because the buyer takes it on, cash is subtracted because the buyer gets to use it.
EV/EBITDA is neutral to leverage and depreciation, which makes it the multiple for comparing companies that borrow differently.
FCF is the basis of every DCF model - learn it before you learn any multiple.

summary.keyIdea: These ten formulas are one chain, not a list: Revenue → FCF → EV → price per share.
summary.formula: EV = Market Cap + Total Debt − Cash;  EV/EBITDA = EV / EBITDA
summary.commonMistake: Adding cash to EV instead of subtracting it, and comparing two differently-leveraged companies on P/E.
summary.action: Take a stock you follow and run the whole chain from revenue down to FCF and back up to EV - on paper, without a spreadsheet.

application.message: Before your next interview, write the chain from Revenue down to FCF on a blank sheet in two minutes. Any line that takes more than five seconds of thought is the line to reread.
application.secondary: In real work this chain is the skeleton of every three-statement model - once you know it, the spreadsheet is only where you type the numbers.
